# The Abolition of Night

There's a story astronomers love to tell, and they admit it may have grown in the telling. On January 17, 1994, an earthquake shook Los Angeles awake before dawn, knocking out power across wide swaths of the city. In the sudden darkness, frightened residents reportedly called 911—not about cracked foundations or burst pipes, but about a strange, vast, silvery cloud hanging over their neighborhoods. The operators couldn't help them. It was the Milky Way. Two million people lived directly beneath our own galaxy, and some of them had never seen it. Their whole lives, the greatest structure visible from Earth had streamed overhead every clear night, dimmed behind streetlight glare, unknown.

Whether the anecdote is precisely true matters less than how readily astronomers believe it. The story rings plausible because it describes us: a species that spent three hundred thousand years reading the dark has, within four generations, nearly forgotten what it says.

For almost the entire span of human history, night was not merely the absence of day. It was a second country—one with its own rules, economies, dangers, and pleasures—that every person alive entered each evening without fail, the way we now enter sleep. The sun set, and humanity crossed a border. What I want to trace here is how thoroughly we razed that border, what the demolition cost, and why it might be worth rebuilding, at least along parts of the frontier.

---

Consider first how expensive light once was. A poor household in early modern England did not flip a switch; it fed a rushlight—a dried rush stalk dipped in kitchen grease—into an iron holder, where it sputtered through perhaps fifteen or twenty minutes of smoky illumination. Tallow candles, made from animal fat, stank and guttered. Beeswax burned clean but cost real money, which is why the great religious houses kept beeswax altar candles blazing while peasants sat by embers. Whale-oil lamps came later and hunted whales for the privilege. Light, in other words, had a price per hour, and ordinary people lived by that ledger.

Whole institutions grew from the expense. The word *curfew* descends from Old French—*couvre-feu*, cover-fire—for the bell rung at dusk when hearths were to be banked. City gates closed at nightfall. London hired linkboys, children carrying flaming torches, to escort paying customers home through lanes with no public lighting at all. Statutes punished "nightwalkers" as a distinct criminal class, on the theory that anyone outside after dark without business was automatically suspect. Night had customs enforcement.

And it had its own physiology. The historian Roger Ekirch, combing diaries, court records, medical texts, and devotional manuals spanning centuries, documented something modern medicine had forgotten: until roughly the nineteenth century, Europeans slept in segments. There was a "first sleep," beginning an hour or two after dusk, followed by a naturally waking interval around midnight—twenty minutes to an hour of quiet lucidity—and then a return to a "second sleep" until dawn. Writers took the pattern so much for granted that Chaucer mentions it in passing. People rose, stoked the fire, prayed—the wakeful window had specialized midnight prayers in the prayer books—interpreted their dreams, which were then credited with prophetic weight, talked softly, or made love, which physicians of the era actually recommended for conception on the grounds that the partners were rested. Anthropologists working in West Africa later found communities whose language divided the night identically. The midnight hour was not insomnia. It was a scheduled room in the house of night, one our species furnished for millennia before the lit bulb evicted us.

None of this should be softened into pastoral fantasy. Night was also feared, and the fear was rational enough. Diseases were blamed on bad air—"mal aria"—that rose with evening damp; the word survives as malaria. Tormenting visions pressed on sleepers' chests and were diagnosed as visits from demons or the "night hag," folk explanations for sleep paralysis that persisted everywhere streetlamps hadn't reached. Watchmen patrolled calling out the hour. Hamlet's father's ghost walks at midnight because everyone knew when the boundary between worlds wore thin. Darkness carried genuine peril, and religions built their tallest towers of prayer against it.

---

But fear was only one chamber of the old night, and the largest room belonged to the stars.

Pre-electric humanity owned, collectively, the finest planetarium imaginable, running every clear night, admission free. The sky was arguably our first text, our first library, our first clock and almanac—the surface on which every culture inscribed its myths and its survival instructions. Egyptian priests watched for the dawn rising of Sirius, whose appearance reliably preceded the Nile's flood, and calibrated an empire on it. Farmers across hemispheres used the Pleiades as a planting and harvest signal; the little cluster rises and sets at just the right moments, everywhere, forever—itinerant agriculture's gift from the sky. Polynesian navigators steered wooden vessels across thousands of open ocean miles using the rising and setting points of memorized stars, holding courses on seas with no landmarks whatsoever. Tell almost any ancient myth and underneath it hums astronomy, because everybody watched the same slow machinery wheeling overhead and needed to explain it to the children.

They also, plainly, saw more. Under a truly dark sky, thousands of stars are visible; the Milky Way shows as a braided river of light, textured, showing dust lanes. Sailors worked full sail by starlight alone. Generations learned constellations from elders as casually as children now learn brand logos. When you understand this, the mythologies stop seeming bizarre. Of course the Pleiades have seven sisters in Australia and Greece and the American plains. Everyone everywhere was raised under the same ceiling and taught the same faint knots of it.

Then we put the ceiling out.

The demolition proceeded in stages. In 1807, spectators gathered along Pall Mall in London to watch a line of gas jets throw a steady artificial glow—among the first public demonstrations of what industry had in store. Within decades, major cities hissed with piped gas and employed armies of lamplighters trundling ladders at dusk. Electricity finished the campaign. By the century's end, arc lamps topped tall poles on city avenues; soon Broadway's marquees earned the district the name the Great White Way. Twenty-four-hour factories proved that night was no longer a wall but a resource—unexploited capacity, shamefully wasted, sensibly filled.

The results are measurable from orbit. Satellite composites of Earth at night show the continents webbed and freckled with light, the eastern United States and western Europe aglow like circuit boards; astronauts describe civilization's glow as looking like a nervous system seen through skin. The 2016 *World Atlas of Artificial Night Sky Brightness* calculated that more than eighty percent of humanity now lives under light-polluted skies. About a third of all people alive—including roughly sixty percent of Europeans and nearly eighty percent of North Americans—cannot see the Milky Way from home. Nor do most realize anything is missing, which is the strangest part: the loss is invisible to those living inside it, like fish petitioning about water. During the Second World War, when blackout regulations forced London dark, newspapers ran pieces wondering at the strange river of light citizens glimpsed overhead—ancient scenery, breaking news.

---

The eviction had tenants besides ourselves, and they have fared worse.

On beaches in Florida, volunteers patrol during hatching season, gathering up baby sea turtles that emerge from the sand, instinct urging them toward the brighter horizon. For two hundred million years, the brighter horizon meant moonlight and star-glint on the sea—the direction of safety. Now the brighter horizon is usually inland: beachfront condos, promenade lamps, parking lots. Volunteers collect the doomed crawlers in buckets at dawn, hundreds of them per season headed for highways and pool drains, and carry them, palmful by palmful, back toward an ocean they will otherwise never reach.

Songbirds migrating at night appear to navigate partly by stellar cues; surveys suggest somewhere in the hundreds of millions die annually in North America from striking illuminated buildings, drawn into disorientation on foggy nights atop glass towers haloed like lighthouses. Moths, which evolved their exquisite nighttime steering over vastly longer timescales than we've been standing upright, hold a constant angle to what they take for the moon; a nearby streetlamp turns that elegant algorithm into a fatal logarithmic spiral around a bulb, night after night, generation after generation—an evolutionary trap sprung in less than two centuries of electric light. Fireflies signal mates with flashes keyed to darkness thresholds; where ambient glow never drops below their minimum, their language goes unread. Corals synchronize mass spawning by moonrise; harbors permanently bright can scramble the rendezvous. Even street trees falter—lit past natural dusk, they hold summer chemistry late and misread the coming winter.

And ourselves. The human body sets its hormones by light. Special cells in the retina, most sensitive to the blue-violet end of the spectrum, feed the internal clock; evening exposure to that band delays the release of melatonin, the hormone that opens sleep's door. Screens deliver it to our faces from a foot away at midnight—historically, an utterly novel situation: each of us now carries a private miniature sun into bed. Large fractions of workers in industrialized nations keep shifts that persistently oppose their clocks; the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies shift work involving circadian disruption as probably carcinogenic. Researchers speak of "social jet lag," the chronic mismatch between biological night and the schedule society demands. We made night disappear and then wondered why we can't rest.

Here is the sour irony: darkness is now a luxury good. Edison is often said to have promised electricity so cheap that only the rich would burn candles; today it's closer to inverted, with the affluent purchasing blackout curtains, darkened suites, retreat lodges positioned at dark-sky sites, and guided stargazing packages, while families beside highway strips live under permanent sodium-orange noon.

---

Before making the case for restoration, fairness requires admitting what the old dark also contained that we're well rid of. Anyone who has lain awake knows that three in the morning has a strange physics. At the bottom of the circadian cycle, the brain amplifies negative weighting; worries metabolize differently, and small debts compound into convictions. Most of what looks like revelation at 3 a.m. reveals itself, at nine, as exhaustion wearing revelation's clothes. A reasonable doctrine follows: the three a.m. mind deserves respect as weather—real, powerful, to be noted and not bargained with.

Yet the borderlands remain astonishing. Mary Shelley, nineteen, trapped indoors during the famously sunless summer of 1816 on Lake Geneva, recalled falling into a waking reverie and watching images arise behind her eyelids: a pale student kneeling beside a thing he had assembled; the thing stirring; the horror of animated clay. She opened her eyes and thought, dreamily, *what terrified me will terrify others*—the seed of *Frankenstein*, germinated in the particular soil of a tired, threshold mind. Others have cultivated that soil deliberately. Edison reportedly napped holding steel balls in his hands above metal pans, so that as he slipped into sleep, muscle relaxation dropped them clanging and woke him to harvest whatever the drowsing brain offered; Dalí did the same with a key held over a plate. These are techniques for skimming the cream off hypnagogia, the shifting corridor between waking and sleep. We pass through it twice a day and almost never look around.

---

What would reconsidering night look like? Encouragingly, people are already doing it. DarkSky International certifies parks, reserves, and entire towns against standards: fixtures fully shielded so light falls where intended rather than skyward; color temperatures shifted warm; sensors and curfews replacing illumination-on-principle. Dozens of protected dark places now span six continents, from cherry-dark observing fields in Pennsylvania to New Zealand's Mackenzie basin, where the southern Milky Way arches so brightly locals complain when visitors applaud at it—applause is common. A French regulation now obliges shops to extinguish their window displays overnight. Tucson retrofitted its streetlights with shielding and adaptive dimming and, by many accounts, thereby regained more sky. Beachside towns switched coastal fixtures to long-wavelength amber that sea turtles' eyes barely register. None of this demands heroic sacrifice; mostly it means aiming light at tasks rather than at the heavens, and remembering that intensity and safety are not synonyms.

For individuals, the restoration begins smaller: an experiment you can conduct on any clear, moonless night. Find a spot as far from streetlight as practical. Put the phone away—an accidental glance at a bright screen resets your eyes' chemical adaptation and can squander thirty-plus minutes of adjustment, since full night vision takes half an hour or more to develop and seconds to undo. Stand and wait. As your retinas recalibrate—rod-dominated, tuned for sensitivity rather than sharpness—you will notice a peculiar fact: faint things vanish when you stare straight at them, because the fovea packs no rods at all. Look slightly to the side of a dim star and it blooms into view. Direct sight, denied; oblique sight, granted.

Take the hint as instruction and apply it generally. The night's oldest lessons tend to arrive this way.

Then lift the practice outward, obliquely, to the galaxy itself. On a sufficiently dark autumn night, aim your averted, patient gaze at a faint gray smear high above Cassiopeia. That patch is the Andromeda Galaxy, the farthest thing unaided human eyes can see—about two and a half million light-years out. The photons landing on your retina left home at a time when our species didn't exist; taming fire, cultivating grain, inventing the sentence—all lie inside their travel time. It is the oldest contact available to a human being, requiring no instrument, costing nothing, delivered continuously for your lifetime and long before it. Somewhere above the Costco parking lot, it is arriving right now.

That may be the sentence to end on—the actual case for abolishing the abolition. Whatever else we did in switching on the lights, we made the universe small, and it is not small. The night's library stands fully stocked exactly where we abandoned it: two hundred million-year-old tidal rhythms, sisters landing in silence, a spiral of suns with Earth's address scratched in pencil in one far suburb. Killing a porch light for one evening is a trivial act. Standing beneath the reopened ceiling until your eyes go native again, feeling your pupils dilate toward capacity, and reading a single page by the light of fires older than speech—that is a reminder of scale, and scale is a rare commodity anymore. The dark is not empty. It never was.
